42914185.text: Non-small cell lung cancer shows wide variability in outcomes after curative-intent resection. 18F-FDG PET/CT is indispensable for staging but primarily reflects glucose metabolism rather than the invasion-related tumor biology that may contribute to recurrence. 68Ga-NOTA-AE105 PET/CT images the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR), a cell-surface mediator of local invasion and metastatic spread. We assessed whether preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET/CT is prognostic for postoperative recurrence. Methods: We conducted a single-center cohort study of patients with resectable lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma who were prospectively enrolled to undergo preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET/CT in addition to standard-of-care 18F-FDG PET/CT. Primary tumor SUVmean and SUVmax were measured for both tracers, and tumor tissue uPAR expression was quantified by immunohistochemistry (H-score). Postoperative recurrence was the primary endpoint and was analyzed in a competing-risks framework with death as a competing event. The primary prognostic analyses evaluated 68Ga-uPAR SUVs, 18F-FDG SUVs, and uPAR H-score as continuous variables using univariable cause-specific Cox models. A 1.5-y horizon was used for exploratory Youden-derived high versus low groups, for which cumulative incidence of recurrence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method. Four patients died without prior recurrence. 68Ga-uPAR uptake correlated with tumor tissue uPAR expression, whereas 18F-FDG uptake did not. As continuous prognostic factors, higher 68Ga-uPAR SUVmax (hazard ratio, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.34-3.49; P = 0.002) and higher uPAR H-score (hazard ratio, 1.04 per unit; 95% CI, 1.01-1.08; P = 0.017) were associated with recurrence; 68Ga-uPAR SUVmean showed borderline evidence of association (P = 0.053), whereas 18F-FDG uptake was not prognostic. Exploratory 1.5-y threshold analyses showed greater early recurrence in the high SUVmean and high H-score groups; the SUVmax comparison did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion: Preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET uptake reflected tumor uPAR expression and was associated with early postoperative recurrence, whereas 18F-FDG uptake was not prognostic in this cohort. These findings suggest that uPAR PET captures invasion-related tumor biology that is not fully reflected by glucose metabolism imaging. External validation is required.

42918885.label: Introduction
42918885.text: Emergency departments face increasing overcrowding, resulting in diagnostic delays, higher mortality, and rising healthcare costs. Early risk stratification is essential to optimise clinical decision-making. Although medical imaging plays a central role in initial assessment, workload pressures and operational constraints have driven the development of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support triage and prioritisation in emergency radiology.

42918885.label: Objective
42918885.text: To map and synthesise evidence on the applications, performance, and limitations of AI in emergency radiology for early risk stratification in acute care.

42918885.label: Materials and methods
42918885.text: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines and Joanna Briggs Institute recommendations. The protocol was developed a priori and registered in the Open Science Framework. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified studies published between 2015 and 2025 that evaluated AI applications in medical imaging in acute care settings. Evidence was synthesised using conceptual mapping and thematic analysis.

42918885.label: Results
42918885.text: Seventy-one studies were included. Computed tomography was the most frequently evaluated modality, followed by radiography and ultrasound. Major domains included neurovascular disease, acute cardiopulmonary conditions, trauma, COVID-19, and acute aortic syndromes. Studies reported high diagnostic performance and potential workflow benefits; however, evidence was predominantly retrospective and internally validated, with limited prospective evaluation, external validation, or evidence of improved patient-level outcomes.

42918885.label: Conclusions
42918885.text: AI applications in emergency radiology show promising diagnostic and workflow-support capabilities. However, current evidence largely reflects early-stage development, with limited prospective validation, scarce real-world impact assessment, and insufficient evaluation of clinically meaningful outcomes.

42918885.label: Key points
42918885.text: Question How clinically mature are AI applications designed to support early risk stratification and prioritisation in time-sensitive emergency radiology workflows? Findings Most studies report high diagnostic performance in time-sensitive conditions, yet evidence remains predominantly retrospective with limited external validation or prospective real-world implementation. Clinical relevance AI may support earlier identification and prioritisation of critical imaging findings, but routine adoption requires prospective external validation and evidence of meaningful effects on clinical decisions and patient outcomes.

42937535.text: Building agents that perceive and act on their environment with a degree of autonomy has long been a focus of artificial intelligence research. This pursuit has become far more practical with the emergence of large language models (LLMs) capable of using natural language to integrate information, follow instructions, and perform forms of reasoning and planning across a wide range of tasks. With its multimodal data streams and orchestrated workflows spanning multiple systems, radiology is uniquely suited to benefit from agents that can adapt to context and automate complex, repetitive tasks. In radiology, LLMs and their multimodal variants have already demonstrated promising performance for individual tasks such as information extraction and report summarization. However, using LLMs in isolation underutilizes their potential to support complex, multistep workflows where decisions depend on evolving context from multiple information sources. Equipping LLMs with external tools and feedback mechanisms enables them to drive systems that exhibit a spectrum of autonomy, ranging from semiautomated workflows to more adaptive agents capable of managing complex processes. This review article examines the design of LLM-driven agentic systems, explores representative radiology applications, discusses evaluation frameworks, and outlines key challenges, including error cascades, tool-use effectiveness, and integration with health information technology infrastructure.

42954785.text: Cardiac myxomas are the second most common benign cardiac tumor in adults. Most arise from the interatrial septum in the left atrium. Although most patients present with cardiac or embolic symptoms, some lesions are detected incidentally at imaging performed for unrelated indications. This case report describes the incidental discovery of a right atrial mass partially visualized at CT of the abdomen and pelvis during workup for cholecystitis. Subsequent multimodality imaging demonstrated a right atrial mass arising from the crista terminalis, which was confirmed to be a myxoma at pathologic examination. This case highlights an atypical origin and location of a common cardiac tumor incidentally detected at abdominal imaging.

43019235.text: A 70-year-old man underwent ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT for evaluation of a pulmonary nodule. He also had a chest wall mass that was initially suspected to represent metastasis. PET/CT images demonstrated that the pulmonary nodule was hypermetabolic, consistent with lung cancer. In contrast, the chest wall mass showed only mild FDG uptake and was interpreted as a benign primary tumor. Pathological examination ultimately confirmed the pulmonary nodule as adenocarcinoma, whereas the chest wall mass was confirmed to be extramedullary hematopoiesis.

43051335.label: Objective
43051335.text: To evaluate the perceptions and preparedness of radiology professionals in Pakistan regarding artificial intelligence (AI) integration in radiology, while exploring leadership perspectives on its future role and implementation challenges.

43051335.label: Methods
43051335.text: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was conducted using consecutive sampling. In phase one, a webinar was held for radiology professionals across Pakistan, followed by pre- and post-webinar surveys assessing participants' knowledge, perceptions, attitudes, and readiness regarding AI integration in radiology. In phase two, a focused group discussion (FGD) with senior radiology leaders was conducted to further explore survey findings. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with p value<0.05 considered statistically significant, while qualitative data underwent thematic framework analysis. Triangulation was performed to integrate and validate findings from both phases.

43051335.label: Results
43051335.text: 132 participants completed both surveys, with nearly half being early-career radiologists. Following the webinar, perceptions toward AI shifted significantly. Disagreement with the statement that AI would replace radiologists increased from 43.9% pre-webinar to 87.9% post-webinar. Support for formal AI training also increased substantially. Self-reported knowledge improved, with participants identifying as "very knowledgeable" increasing from 4.5% to 25% after the session (p=0.003). FGD findings highlighted concerns regarding governance, infrastructure, local validation of AI tools, and limited technical expertise.

43051335.label: Conclusion
43051335.text: Radiology professionals in Pakistan, particularly early-career practitioners, show growing enthusiasm toward AI integration when supported by structured education and training. Leadership perspectives further emphasize the need for locally validated AI solutions, stronger governance frameworks, and integration of AI into radiology curricula for sustainable implementation in low- and middle-income countries.

43066785.label: Purpose
43066785.text: To develop a machine-learning model combining multiparametric MRI-derived intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) scores with clinical features for preoperative prediction of microsatellite instability (MSI) in rectal cancer and to explore MSI-associated molecular features.

43066785.label: Methods
43066785.text: This retrospective study enrolled 464 rectal cancer patients from three centers, including training (n = 198; MSI-H, 26), internal validation (n = 110; MSI-H, 12), and external validation (n = 156; MSI-H, 23) cohorts. Three-dimensional ITH scores were derived from T2WI and DWI. Logistic regression identified independent clinical predictors. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to construct clinical, ITH, and combined models. Performance was assessed using AUCs with 95% confidence intervals, calibration curves, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP. TCGA transcriptomics, PPI analysis, and immunohistochemistry in 10 local samples were used for molecular exploration.

43066785.label: Results
43066785.text: Age, tumor length, location, and N stage were independent predictors. The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.865 (95% CI, 0.828-0.899), 0.839 (95% CI, 0.775-0.895), and 0.785 (95% CI, 0.729-0.835) in training, internal, and external cohorts, respectively. In external validation, it was comparable to the clinical model (AUC = 0.790; BH-adjusted P = 0.076), and the ITH-only model performed poorly (AUC = 0.548). SHAP identified tumor location, T stage, and ITH features as major contributors. Transcriptomics identified 378 differentially expressed genes, and PPI analysis suggested AKT1 as a hub candidate. IHC showed higher AKT1 H-scores in MSS tumors (143.60 ± 26.14 vs. 76.74 ± 38.43; P = 0.008).

43066785.label: Conclusion
43066785.text: The model showed favorable training/internal performance but moderate external performance without clear incremental value. Larger prospective multicenter cohorts are needed. Transcriptomic and pilot IHC analyses suggest possible AKT1 expression differences between MSI-H and MSS rectal cancers.

43071585.label: Purpose
43071585.text: Centiloid (CL) scaling quantifies amyloid-β plaque burden in Alzheimer disease, but its utility in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is uncertain. We evaluated the ability of CL to discriminate probable CAA from deep perforator arteriopathy (DPA) among patients with small vessel disease (SVD) and examined its associations with neuroimaging markers and cognition.

43071585.label: Methods
43071585.text: We enrolled 92 patients with probable CAA and 27 patients with DPA. CL values were derived from [11C]PiB PET. Classification performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic and decision curve analyses. Associations with MRI markers and cognitive function were examined using correlation and regression models.

43071585.label: Results
43071585.text: CL scaling showed good discrimination between CAA and DPA (AUC: 0.837, 95% CI: 0.733-0.905). A cutoff of 5.2 yielded 78.3% sensitivity and 88.9% specificity. Higher CL values were associated with lobar microbleed burden (P<0.001), cortical superficial siderosis (P=0.002), and centrum semiovale enlarged perivascular spaces (P=0.007), as well as the CAA score (P<0.001), but not the total SVD score. After covariate adjustment, higher CL values were independently associated with lower MMSE scores (β=-0.048, P=0.025) and a trend toward greater CDR severity (OR=1.012, P=0.052). Adding CL to a clinical-MRI model improved discrimination (ΔAUC=0.077, 95% CI: 0.010-0.175, P=0.025).

43071585.label: Conclusions
43071585.text: CL scaling discriminates clinically defined probable CAA from DPA in sporadic SVD. Higher CL values are associated with greater CAA-related MRI burden and worse cognitive performance.
